lead.question: Let a(n) count first-quadrant vertex-self-avoiding walks from (0,0) to (n,0) with steps (0,1),(1,0),(1,1),(−1,1),(1,−1). At the departure vertex forbid vertical steps below y=x and horizontal steps above it. For all n≥4 prove a(n)−a(n−1)+(−n²−n+3)a(n−2)+(2−n)a(n−3)+(n−2)(n−3)a(n−4)=0, or give an exact counterexample.
lead.title: A284230: Number of self-avoiding planar walks starting at (0,0), ending at (n,0), remaining in the first quadrant and using steps (0,1), (1
lead.decisive_test: The sum x+y never decreases. On each antidiagonal the walk therefore traverses just one interval, monotonically. Enumerate by entry and exit of that interval using integer arithmetic; derive from this a smaller parity-dependent transition or exhibit the first failure. A short parity recurrence is already posted as code: establish its combinatorial validity before eliminating parity.
lead.blocker: Proving the parity formula depends on a walk-to-recurrence derivation. Existing Maple code implements the counts but gives no derivation in the OEIS entry. Check the author’s related row-refined triangle and literature. Do not count algebraic elimination by itself as a proof from the walk definition.

review.statement: For each integer n ≥ 0, let a(n) count walks from (0,0) to (n,0) whose vertices have nonnegative integer coordinates and are pairwise distinct. The allowed steps are (0,1), (1,0), (1,1), (−1,1), and (1,−1). At the departure vertex, forbid (0,1) when y < x and (1,0) when y > x. For every integer n ≥ 4, the claim is a(n) − a(n−1) + (−n²−n+3)a(n−2) + (2−n)a(n−3) + (n−2)(n−3)a(n−4) = 0.
review.significance: The candidate proof derives the parity recurrence in the OEIS code directly from the walks and then proves Mathar’s fourth-order recurrence.
review.settlement_test: Verify the unique decomposition at the first entry into the final level and the algebraic elimination below. A refutation would require one integer n ≥ 4 with exact walk counts yielding a nonzero residual.
review.aliases: OEIS A284230 and the row sums of Heinz’s length-refined triangle A284414, also listed by columns as A284652. A284461 is the even subsequence, which counts walks ending on the diagonal. [A284414](https://oeis.org/A284414), [A284652](https://oeis.org/A284652), [A284461](https://oeis.org/A284461).
review.attempt:
Alois P. Heinz authored A284230 in March 2017. The entry gives the parity recurrence in Maple and credits Indranil Ghosh with a Mathematica implementation. It credits R. J. Mathar with the April 2017 fourth-order conjecture. No earlier proof from the walk definition surfaced in the sources consulted. Marcus Lawson and Mark van Hoeij discuss the conjectured recurrence in §7.1 of their 2026 ISSAC paper and investigate the associated difference operator. [A284230](https://oeis.org/A284230), [Global Curvature of Difference Operators](https://doi.org/10.1145/3815436.3815439).

Direct enumeration in the isolated JavaScript execution cell tracked visited vertices and counted 1, 2, 5, 24, 111, 762, 5127, 45588, 400593, 4370634 for n = 0 through 9. Exact integer arithmetic gave zero residuals for n = 4 through 9. No `/agent.txt` was found at the root or in the workspace. The Left to Solve page was inaccessible, so I used the supplied statement and the original OEIS entry.
review.proof_or_witness:
Let L_m consist of the m+1 vertices with x+y=m. A walk’s level never decreases. Its portion on any one level is a path on a line of adjacent vertices, since the two level-preserving steps change x by ±1. A reversal repeats a vertex. Thus, from its first vertex on L_m, the walk has exactly one possible suffix on that level to each prescribed endpoint, including the empty suffix when the two vertices coincide. The earlier portion lies strictly below L_m and cannot intersect that suffix. Cutting at the first vertex on L_m therefore gives a bijection between first-entry prefixes and walks to any fixed vertex of L_m. Consequently every vertex of L_m has exactly a(m) walks ending there.

For n ≥ 2, a first-entry prefix into L_n arrives either from L_{n−1} by a step increasing the level by one or from L_{n−2} by (1,1). Each of the n vertices on L_{n−1} has one allowed step increasing the level by one, with one additional choice at the diagonal vertex if n is odd. Every one of the n−1 vertices on L_{n−2} has one (1,1) step. These steps all land in the quadrant and reach a fresh level. Counting prefixes followed by the unique suffix to (n,0) gives a(n)=c_n a(n−1)+(n−1)a(n−2), where c_n=n+(n mod 2). The same count on the first two levels gives a(0)=1 and a(1)=2.

For n ≥ 4, apply the parity recurrence at n and n−1 to obtain a(n)−a(n−1) = [(c_n−1)c_{n−1}+n−1]a(n−2)+(n−2)(c_n−1)a(n−3). Both parities give (c_n−1)c_{n−1}=n(n−1), and c_n−1=c_{n−2}+1. Applying the recurrence at n−2 gives c_{n−2}a(n−3)=a(n−2)−(n−3)a(n−4). Substitution yields a(n)−a(n−1)=(n²+n−3)a(n−2)+(n−2)a(n−3)−(n−2)(n−3)a(n−4), as required.
review.remaining_obligation: Independently check that first-entry prefixes can be extended to every endpoint on their final level without repeating a vertex, that the extra one-level step occurs exactly when n is odd, and that all recurrence applications are valid at n=4. The candidate argument covers every n in scope and awaits independent review. The shortlist verdict carries no automatic solution credit.
